doc.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005

title: Toscanini and Stokowski and the Shostakovich Seventh
summary: Premiering the Shostakovich Seventh on a borrowed low-C bass clarinet, under both conductors.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: I wanted to ask you about — you’ve played with an awful lot of great conductors.

Stokowski. Well let me tell you about the two conductors. They used to alternate. One week on the broadcast Toscanini conducted. The next week Stokowski. And they alternated. Now we premiered the Shostakovitch Seventh Symphony. It can be bought. It was taken off the air. And I had to borrow a special bass clarinet that went down to the low C. Today they all go to the low C. So I was tipped off by the bassoon player, that Mike Guerra in Philadelphia, had one, it went to the low C. I called him and he says, “Yes I’ll gladly loan it to you.” And we did it with Toscanini. I had plenty of wind in those days, but still, down there, the wind was hard, you know? And Toscanini didn’t budge, didn’t budge. He just kept conducting. Six months later or so we repeated it with Stokowski playing. And he gets on the podium and he says, “Now bass clarinet and oboe, take your time, I’ll wait for you.” And it was much easier with Stokowski. He didn’t rush you, you know? I never forgot that.
So actually we did it twice within six months. But the one with Toscanini is the one that they released. It can be bought.
